# Separate browser and transport trust boundaries

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `security-browser-transport` · **Security & Identity** · Catalog level: foundation

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S05-Q015](#S05-Q015)

<p>How would you distinguish CORS, CSRF and XSS when reviewing a browser application’s security?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Review a browser-to-API interaction by matching each security risk to the boundary it crosses.</p>

<ul>
<li>Explain transport protection and where it ends.</li>
<li>Trace a TLS connection setup and a failed trust check.</li>
<li>Distinguish cross-origin browser policy from CSRF/XSS attack scenarios using interaction and credential behavior.</li>
<li>Check that diagnostic paths do not expose credentials or private data.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>Follow the interaction from the network connection to browser behavior and application logs. Transport trust establishes one boundary; browser-originated actions and untrusted content introduce others. The final questions examine whether the diagnostic evidence creates a new exposure.</p>

### S05-Q013 · Foundation

<p>How do HTTP and HTTPS differ technically, and what protection does that difference provide to an API client?</p>

**Source:** [S05-Q013](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q013)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S05-Q013](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q013)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare HTTP and HTTPS technically.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Explain the communication boundary being protected. Keep transport protection separate from application permissions and trusted endpoint behavior.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Describe a transport guarantee together with its limits.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a client-to-server connection; identify any intermediary where transport protection ends.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains what changes on the network path in a concrete request.</li>
<li>Identifies a security risk that remains and how its control would be checked.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming HTTPS makes every application action safe without discussing endpoint or access risks.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What must you examine when HTTPS terminates at a reverse proxy?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S05-Q014 · Mechanism

<p>What is the TLS handshake trying to establish before application data is exchanged?</p>

**Source:** [S05-Q014](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q014)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S05-Q014](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q014)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain the purpose of the TLS handshake at a high level.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Give a high-level causal sequence: the parties involved, what they must agree on, and the point at which the client can proceed or reject the connection.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain a connection setup mechanism and one failure boundary.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the TLS version and whether client authentication is required; message details vary by version. Establish the deployed version/provider and consult official documentation before answering.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects handshake steps to trust and protected communication rather than listing packet names.</li>
<li>Explains a failed trust check and how to observe the resulting connection behavior.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Memorizing one message sequence and presenting it as identical across TLS versions.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you investigate a client rejecting the server certificate?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S05-Q015"></a>

### S05-Q015 · Application

<p>How would you distinguish CORS, CSRF and XSS when reviewing a browser application’s security?</p>

**Source:** [S05-Q015](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q015)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S05-Q015](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q015)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain CORS, CSRF and XSS as distinct concerns.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Distinguish the cross-origin browser access policy from CSRF and XSS attack scenarios. For each, describe the legitimate or hostile interaction, credential behavior and boundary to inspect; expand abbreviations when introducing them.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish a browser access policy from attack scenarios and justify relevant controls with their limits.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Clarify origins, credential handling and whether untrusted content is rendered; use separate examples rather than one universal defense.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains a distinct causal scenario for each concern.</li>
<li>Proposes a check that tests the chosen protection and states a remaining boundary.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating a CORS setting as proof that all browser-originated attacks are prevented.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would changing from explicit credentials to automatically sent cookies affect your threat analysis?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S05-Q017 · Production decision

<p>What security-sensitive information should application logs exclude, and how would you keep those logs useful for diagnosis?</p>

**Source:** [S05-Q017](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q017)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S05-Q017](../../sources/05-security-cloud-devops.md#q017)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What security-sensitive information must not be written to logs?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Review a hypothetical request and error log. Identify information that exposes credentials or private data, then explain the diagnostic need that remains.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Balance diagnostic evidence with credential and privacy protection.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Consider request headers, bodies, exceptions and telemetry destinations; use fictional examples without actual sensitive data.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Names concrete exposure paths and explains the risk of each.</li>
<li>Proposes a way to test logging behavior in success and error paths.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Saying “do not log secrets” while leaving headers or exception payloads unexamined.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you detect a credential accidentally included in an exception log?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>An Angular application calls an API through an HTTPS-terminating proxy, sends credentials and renders user-supplied text. A support feature captures failed request details. Draw the boundaries, create separate attack or failure scenarios and propose checks for transport, browser behavior and logging. Establish the actual TLS and credential configuration before making implementation claims.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Defines HTTP/HTTPS, TLS, CORS, CSRF and XSS, and recognizes sensitive logging information.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Explains distinct causal threats and matching controls with their limits; tests failure paths and credential exposure across the actual boundaries.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>A padlock icon, CORS configuration or a statement that secrets are not logged does not prove the other boundaries are protected.</p>
